records.greek: Καὶ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ τρίτῃ γάμος ἐγένετο ἐν Κανὰ τῆς Γαλιλαίας, καὶ ἦν ἡ μήτηρ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἐκεῖ·
records.gloss: And on the day the third a wedding took place in Cana of the Galilee, and was the mother of the Jesus there.

L.1: And on the third day a wedding took place in Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there.

R.1: Two days later there was a wedding in the village of Cana in Galilee. Jesus's mother was there.

decisions.choice: on the third day, counted from the last day named (1:43): two days later
alternatives: the third day of the week
decisions.reason: Days were counted inclusively, so the day of the last event counts as the first. John has been marking days since 1:29, 1:35 and 1:43; this continues the count.

decisions.choice: a plain time note that may also carry an echo
alternatives: a deliberate pointer to the resurrection
decisions.reason: "The third day" is the day of the resurrection (compare 2:19 "in three days"), and on the third day God showed himself at Sinai (Exodus 19:11, 16), while this sign reveals Jesus's glory (2:11). John does not draw either link himself, so every level keeps the phrase and makes no claim. Readable gives the plain sense.

decisions.choice: a wedding celebration
decisions.reason: The word covers the whole celebration, a feast that could last several days (Judges 14:12, 17). The groom's family provided the food and wine for the guests.

decisions.choice: the mother of Jesus / Jesus's mother, not "Mary"
decisions.reason: John never gives her name (here and at 19:25-27); every level keeps his description.

decisions.choice: Two days later
decisions.reason: The plain sense of the inclusive count (m1). Literal and Balanced keep "third day" so that the possible echo (m2) stays visible.

records.heading: The wedding at Cana

records.greek: ἐκλήθη δὲ καὶ ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸν γάμον.
records.gloss: Was invited and also the Jesus and the disciples of him to the wedding.

L.2: And Jesus also was invited, and His disciples, to the wedding.

R.2: Jesus and His disciples had been invited to the wedding too.

decisions.choice: Jesus is the main guest; the disciples come with him
alternatives: Jesus and the disciples invited as equals
decisions.reason: The verb is singular and agrees with Jesus, who is named first; the disciples are added after him.

decisions.choice: the disciples who had begun to follow him in 1:35-51
decisions.reason: John has not yet mentioned the Twelve (first at 6:67). The disciples here are those of chapter 1, among them Andrew, Simon Peter, Philip and Nathanael, who came from Cana (21:2).

records.greek: καὶ ὑστερήσαντος οἴνου λέγει ἡ μήτηρ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ πρὸς αὐτόν· Οἶνον οὐκ ἔχουσιν.
records.gloss: And having run short wine, says the mother of the Jesus to him, "Wine not they have."

L.3: And when [the] wine ran short, the mother of Jesus says to Him, "They have no wine."

R.3: When the wine was all gone, Jesus's mother came to Him and said, "They have run out of wine."

decisions.choice: running out of wine would shame the host family
decisions.reason: Hospitality was a serious duty, and the groom's family was expected to provide for the guests through the whole feast (m3 at 2:1). Running out was a public embarrassment.

decisions.choice: a statement of need that hints at a request
alternatives: a direct request for a miracle
decisions.reason: She only states the problem, but she says it to Jesus, and verse 5 shows that she expects him to do something. No level turns it into an explicit request.

decisions.choice: when the wine ran short (SBLGNT)
alternatives: a longer reading: they had no wine, because the wine of the wedding was used up
decisions.reason: The longer wording is found in the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus and some Old Latin manuscripts. It says the same thing at more length, so the shorter text of the great majority is kept and no footnote is needed. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: said
decisions.reason: John often tells a story in the present tense ("she says") for vividness; here and in the rest of the passage Balanced and Readable use the past, which is normal for a story told in this language. Literal keeps the present.

decisions.choice: came to him and said
decisions.reason: Readable shows that she brings the problem to him; the words add a movement implied by "to him".

records.greek: καὶ λέγει αὐτῇ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί, γύναι;
records.gloss: And says to her the Jesus, "What to me and to you, woman?"

L.4: And Jesus says to her, "What [is that] to Me and to you, Woman?

R.4: Jesus answered, "Mother, why are you bringing this to Me?

decisions.choice: a courteous refusal to be directed: it is not hers to set his course
alternatives: that is no concern of ours (the shortage does not concern us)
decisions.reason: The phrase, literally "what to me and to you", marks distance between two parties. It can be hostile (Judges 11:12; Mark 1:24) or a mild putting-off (2 Kings 3:13; 2 Samuel 16:10). Since Jesus does act, he is not indifferent to the need; he is saying that what he does is set by his hour (the next sentence), not by a family request. The evidence for how sharp it is is balanced.

decisions.choice: Woman: a respectful address
decisions.reason: The address is courteous; Jesus uses it to the Samaritan woman (4:21), to Mary Magdalene (20:15) and to his mother from the cross (19:26). It is unusual for a son to use it to his mother, and the distance it sets matches the idiom (m1). The same address returns at the cross, when his hour has come.

decisions.choice: Woman
decisions.reason: "Woman" on its own can sound cold, but keeping it lets readers connect 2:4 with 19:26; the footnote says it was respectful. "Dear woman" would add warmth the word does not carry by itself.

decisions.choice: Mother
decisions.reason: For young readers "Woman" sounds rude, which the Greek is not. She is his mother, so Readable uses the address a son would use. The footnote gives the literal word.

decisions.choice: is that a matter for you and me? (B); why are you bringing this to me? (R)
alternatives: What is that to me and to you? (Literal)
decisions.reason: Both keep the idiom a question and keep its distance without making it rude; Readable says it plainly.

records.greek: οὔπω ἥκει ἡ ὥρα μου.
records.gloss: Not yet has come the hour of me.

L.4: My hour has not yet come."

R.4: My time has not come yet."

decisions.choice: his hour: the time the Father has set, which John later shows to be his death and glorification
alternatives: only the right moment to act at this wedding
decisions.reason: This is the first mention of Jesus's hour. Later it "had not yet come" (7:30; 8:20) until "the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified" (12:23; 13:1; 17:1). At Cana the sign shows his glory ahead of time (2:11). The hour is set by the Father, not by request.

decisions.choice: a statement
alternatives: a question: has my hour not come?
decisions.reason: The manuscripts have no punctuation, and some early readers took it as a question. The SBLGNT punctuates it as a statement, and John's other uses of "not yet" with the hour are statements (7:30; 8:20).

decisions.choice: My time
decisions.reason: Readable says "time" because "hour" sounds like sixty minutes; Literal and Balanced keep "hour" so the thread through the Gospel stays visible.

records.greek: λέγει ἡ μήτηρ αὐτοῦ τοῖς διακόνοις· Ὅ τι ἂν λέγῃ ὑμῖν ποιήσατε.
records.gloss: Says the mother of him to the servants, "Whatever he may say to you, do."

L.5: His mother says to the servants, "Whatever He says to you, do [it]."

R.5: His mother said to the servants, "Do anything He tells you."

decisions.choice: an echo of Pharaoh's words about Joseph
decisions.reason: In the Greek Old Testament Pharaoh tells the hungry Egyptians, "Go to Joseph, and whatever he says to you, do" (Genesis 41:55). The wording is nearly the same. In both stories a need is met through the one others are told to obey.

decisions.choice: the household servants waiting on the feast
decisions.reason: The word means a servant or attendant; the church sense came later. The same people are called servants in verse 9.

decisions.choice: she trusts him to act, though he has just put her off
decisions.reason: Her words show she takes his reply as leaving room for him to act in his own way.

records.greek: ἦσαν δὲ ἐκεῖ λίθιναι ὑδρίαι ἓξ κατὰ τὸν καθαρισμὸν τῶν Ἰουδαίων κείμεναι, χωροῦσαι ἀνὰ μετρητὰς δύο ἢ τρεῖς.
records.gloss: Were now there stone water jars six, according to the purification of the Jews standing, holding each measures two or three.

L.6: Now there were six stone water jars standing there according to the purification [rites] of the Jews, holding two or three measures each.

R.6: Six large stone jars for water were standing nearby. The Jewish people used jars like these for religious washing. Each jar held about 20 to 30 gallons.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the Jewish people and their customs
decisions.reason: John uses the word in several senses (see the note on the book's terms). Here it names the people whose purity customs these were; John explains them for readers who did not share them. Jesus, his mother and his disciples are Jews.

decisions.choice: stone jars kept for the washings that made people and vessels ritually clean
decisions.reason: Jewish custom washed hands and vessels before meals (Mark 7:3-4). Stone was used because, unlike clay, it was held not to become unclean (compare Leviticus 11:33, where an unclean clay pot must be broken). Stone vessels are common finds in first-century Judea and Galilee.

decisions.choice: two or three measures each: about 80 to 120 liters
decisions.reason: The measure named, μετρητής, was a liquid measure of about 39 liters. Each jar held two or three of them, so the six jars together held roughly 480 to 700 liters. The amount of wine in the sign is lavish.

decisions.choice: about {{units:20 to 30 gallons|two or three measures}}
alternatives: two or three measures at every level
twenty to thirty gallons in words
decisions.reason: The Greek measure (about 10 gallons, or 39 liters) means nothing to most readers, so Balanced and Readable give the modern equivalent by default, and the units setting shows the original "two or three measures". Numerals are used in measurements. Literal always keeps the ancient unit.

decisions.choice: Jewish / the Jewish people
decisions.reason: Where the word means the people, Balanced and Readable use "Jewish" (see the book's terms).

records.greek: λέγει αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Γεμίσατε τὰς ὑδρίας ὕδατος· καὶ ἐγέμισαν αὐτὰς ἕως ἄνω.
records.gloss: Says to them the Jesus, "Fill the jars with water." And they filled them up to above.

L.7: Jesus says to them, "Fill the jars with water." And they filled them up to [the] top.

R.7: Jesus told the servants, "Fill the jars with water." So they filled the jars all the way to the top.

decisions.choice: filled to the brim
decisions.reason: The servants filled the jars completely, so nothing else could have been added and the amount was as large as the jars allowed (2:6).

decisions.choice: the servants
decisions.reason: Readable names the people meant by "them" (verse 5).

records.greek: καὶ λέγει αὐτοῖς· Ἀντλήσατε νῦν καὶ φέρετε τῷ ἀρχιτρικλίνῳ· οἱ δὲ ἤνεγκαν.
records.gloss: And he says to them, "Draw out now and carry to the master of the feast." And they carried.
pieces: man in charge of the feast

L.8: And He says to them, "Draw [some] out now and carry [it] to the master of the feast." And they carried [it].

R.8: Then He said, "Now take some out and bring it to the man in charge of the feast." So they did.

decisions.choice: the man presiding over the feast, in charge of the food and drink
alternatives: a guest chosen to preside over the drinking (compare Sirach 32:1-2)
decisions.reason: The word means the head of the dining room. Whether he was a senior servant or an honored guest is not clear, but either way he was responsible for the meal and could judge the wine.

decisions.choice: draw some out, most naturally from the jars just filled
alternatives: draw from the well, the jars being left full
decisions.reason: The verb is used of drawing water from a well (4:7, 15), and some read it so here. But nothing in the story mentions a well, and the order follows straight on from filling the jars. Every level says only "draw" or "take some out" without naming the source.

decisions.choice: the man in charge of the feast
decisions.reason: Plain words that fit either view of his role (m1).

records.greek: ὡς δὲ ἐγεύσατο ὁ ἀρχιτρίκλινος τὸ ὕδωρ οἶνον γεγενημένον, καὶ οὐκ ᾔδει πόθεν ἐστίν, οἱ δὲ διάκονοι ᾔδεισαν οἱ ἠντληκότες τὸ ὕδωρ, φωνεῖ τὸν νυμφίον ὁ ἀρχιτρίκλινος καὶ λέγει αὐτῷ· Πᾶς ἄνθρωπος πρῶτον τὸν καλὸν οἶνον τίθησιν, καὶ ὅταν μεθυσθῶσιν τὸν ἐλάσσω· σὺ τετήρηκας τὸν καλὸν οἶνον ἕως ἄρτι.
records.gloss: When then tasted the master of the feast the water wine having become, and not he knew from where it is, but the servants knew, the ones having drawn the water, calls the bridegroom the master of the feast \v 10 and says to him, "Every man first the good wine sets, and when they have become drunk, the lesser; you have kept the good wine until now."
pieces: The man in charge of the feast

L.9: And when the master of the feast tasted the water that had become wine, and did not know where it was from (but the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast calls the bridegroom
L.10: and says to him, "Everyone sets out the good wine first, and when [the guests] have become drunk, the lesser [wine]; you have kept the good wine until now."

R.9: The man in charge of the feast tasted the water. It had turned into wine! He did not know where it had come from, but the servants who had taken out the water knew. So he called the bridegroom over.
R.10: He said, "A host always serves the good wine first. Then, when the guests have drunk so much that they cannot tell the difference, he serves the cheaper wine. But you have kept the good wine until now!"

decisions.choice: the water had really become wine
alternatives: the water only seemed to be wine
decisions.reason: The perfect participle describes a finished change: what was water now was wine. John does not say when or how it happened, only that it had.

decisions.choice: he did not know where it came from
decisions.reason: "Where from" is a question John keeps returning to about Jesus himself (7:27-28; 9:29-30; 19:9). The servants know; the man in charge does not.

decisions.choice: drunk: their taste is dulled
alternatives: have drunk freely, without being drunk
decisions.reason: The verb normally means to be drunk (Acts 2:15; 1 Thessalonians 5:7). The man in charge is stating a general rule about what hosts usually do, not saying that the guests at Cana were drunk.

decisions.choice: he speaks to the bridegroom because the groom's household provided the wine
decisions.reason: The bridegroom gets the credit for wine he did not provide.

decisions.choice: every host: anyone giving a feast
decisions.reason: "Every person" here is a general rule about whoever gives a feast; it is not limited to men.

decisions.choice: Every host / A host
decisions.reason: The general word for a person refers to whoever gives the feast, so "host" says it plainly and needs no setting. Literal keeps the general word with the gender setting.

decisions.choice: the good wine
decisions.reason: The Greek has the plain adjective "good", not a superlative. Keeping "good" also keeps the repeated word that ties the rule to the man's surprise.

decisions.choice: drunk so much that they cannot tell the difference
decisions.reason: Readable spells out why hosts do this, which the rule implies (m3).

records.greek: ταύτην ἐποίησεν ἀρχὴν τῶν σημείων ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐν Κανὰ τῆς Γαλιλαίας καὶ ἐφανέρωσεν τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐπίστευσαν εἰς αὐτὸν οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: This did [as] beginning of the signs the Jesus in Cana of the Galilee and revealed the glory of him, and believed in him the disciples of him.

L.11: This, [the] beginning of the signs, Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and He revealed His glory, and His disciples believed in Him.

R.11: This was the first sign Jesus did. It happened at Cana in Galilee. By it He showed His glory, and His disciples believed in Him.

decisions.choice: the first, the beginning of the signs
alternatives: merely the first in a numbered list
decisions.reason: The word is "beginning", not just "first": it opens the series of signs that runs through the Gospel. John counts the second at 4:54.

decisions.choice: sign: a deed that points beyond itself to who Jesus is
decisions.reason: John's word stresses meaning, not power. He gathers the purpose of the signs at the end: they are written so that readers may believe (20:30-31).

decisions.choice: he made his glory visible
decisions.reason: This takes up 1:14, "we have seen his glory". The glory is God's presence shown in Jesus, here in an abundant gift.

decisions.choice: believed in him: put their trust in him
decisions.reason: "Believe in" with a person, John's usual phrase, means trusting the person, not only accepting a fact. Their response is the one the signs aim at; contrast 2:23-24.

decisions.choice: In it
decisions.reason: Balanced shows that the glory was revealed through this sign; the Greek joins the clauses with a plain "and".

records.greek: Μετὰ τοῦτο κατέβη εἰς Καφαρναοὺμ αὐτὸς καὶ ἡ μήτηρ αὐτοῦ καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ καὶ οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐκεῖ ἔμειναν οὐ πολλὰς ἡμέρας.
records.gloss: After this went down to Capernaum he and the mother of him and the brothers and the disciples of him, and there they stayed not many days.

L.12: After this He went down to Capernaum, He and His mother and the brothers and His disciples, and there they stayed not many days.

R.12: After this, Jesus went down to the town of Capernaum with His mother, His brothers and His disciples. They stayed there only a few days.

decisions.choice: went down: from the hill country to the lakeshore
decisions.reason: Capernaum lay on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, well below Cana in the hills.

decisions.choice: brothers
decisions.reason: The word is the ordinary one for brothers, and his brothers appear again in 7:3-10. Christians differ on whether they were sons of Mary, sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage, or close relatives; the text does not settle it, so every level says "brothers". Specific men are meant here, so the gender setting does not apply.

decisions.choice: not many days: only a few days
decisions.reason: An understatement for a short stay; the next verse moves on to Passover in Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus at the start of a new scene.

records.greek: Καὶ ἐγγὺς ἦν τὸ πάσχα τῶν Ἰουδαίων, καὶ ἀνέβη εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα ὁ Ἰησοῦς.
records.gloss: And near was the Passover of the Jews, and went up to Jerusalem the Jesus.

L.13: And the Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.

R.13: The Jewish Passover festival was coming soon, so Jesus traveled up to Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the Jewish people, whose festival it was
decisions.reason: John explains Jewish festivals for readers who did not keep them (also 6:4; 11:55). The phrase does not set Jesus apart from his people: he goes up to keep the feast.

decisions.choice: Passover: the spring festival recalling the exodus from Egypt
decisions.reason: Passover remembered God's rescue of Israel from Egypt (Exodus 12), and Jewish men were to go up to the sanctuary for it (Deuteronomy 16:16). John names three Passovers (2:13; 6:4; 11:55); at the last Jesus dies.

decisions.choice: went up: Jerusalem is high in the hills
decisions.reason: One always "goes up" to Jerusalem (Psalm 122:4), as one goes down to Capernaum (2:12).

decisions.choice: Jewish
decisions.reason: The word means the people here, so Balanced and Readable say "Jewish" (see the book's terms).

decisions.choice: so
decisions.reason: Readable shows that he went to keep the feast, which the context implies.

records.heading: Jesus clears the temple

records.greek: καὶ εὗρεν ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ τοὺς πωλοῦντας βόας καὶ πρόβατα καὶ περιστερὰς καὶ τοὺς κερματιστὰς καθημένους, καὶ ποιήσας φραγέλλιον ἐκ σχοινίων πάντας ἐξέβαλεν ἐκ τοῦ ἱεροῦ τά τε πρόβατα καὶ τοὺς βόας, καὶ τῶν κολλυβιστῶν ἐξέχεεν τὰ κέρματα καὶ τὰς τραπέζας ἀνέστρεψεν, καὶ τοῖς τὰς περιστερὰς πωλοῦσιν εἶπεν· Ἄρατε ταῦτα ἐντεῦθεν, μὴ ποιεῖτε τὸν οἶκον τοῦ πατρός μου οἶκον ἐμπορίου.
records.gloss: And he found in the temple the ones selling oxen and sheep and doves and the money changers sitting, \v 15 and having made a whip out of cords, all he drove out from the temple, the both sheep and the oxen, and of the money changers he poured out the coins and the tables overturned, \v 16 and to the ones the doves selling he said, "Take these things from here; not make the house of the Father of me a house of trade."

L.14: And in the temple He found those selling cattle and sheep and doves, and the money changers sitting [there],
L.15: and having made a whip out of cords, He drove all out of the temple, both the sheep and the cattle, and He poured out the coins of the money changers and overturned the tables,
L.16: and to those selling the doves He said, "Take these things from here; do not make the house of My Father a house of trade."

R.14: In the temple courtyard Jesus found people selling cattle, sheep and doves for sacrifices. Others were sitting there changing money.
R.15: So Jesus made a whip out of ropes. He chased all of them out of the temple area, both sheep and cattle. He threw the money changers' coins on the ground and knocked over their tables.
R.16: He told the people selling doves, "Take these things out of here! Stop using My Father's house as a place to buy and sell!"

decisions.choice: the temple area as a whole, with its outer courts
decisions.reason: This word names the whole temple complex, including the large outer court where trade went on. In verses 19-21 Jesus uses a different word, for the sanctuary itself.

decisions.choice: a market serving pilgrims
alternatives: private trade with no link to worship
decisions.reason: Pilgrims needed animals without defect for sacrifice; doves were the offering of the poor (Leviticus 5:7; 12:8). The temple tax had to be paid in an approved coin (Exodus 30:13), so money changers exchanged coins. The trade served worship, but it was being done inside the temple courts.

decisions.choice: he drove them all out, the sheep and cattle included; whether the sellers are meant as well is left open
alternatives: only the animals were driven out
the sellers and the animals were driven out
decisions.reason: "All" is masculine and is followed by "both the sheep and the cattle", which may explain it or add to it. The whip of cords suits driving animals; the text does not say he struck anyone. Every level keeps "all" without deciding.

decisions.choice: my Father's house: Jesus calls God his own Father
alternatives: the house of our father (Israel's God, in general)
decisions.reason: The first time in John that Jesus calls God "my Father" (compare Luke 2:49). The authorities' challenge in verse 18 responds to the authority he claims.

decisions.choice: possibly an echo of Zechariah 14:21
decisions.reason: Zechariah's vision of the last day ends, "there will no longer be a trader in the house of the LORD". The link is in the idea, not the wording, so it is uncertain.

decisions.choice: temple courts / temple courtyard / temple area
decisions.reason: Distinguishes the temple area from the sanctuary (m1), which keeps the word "temple" clear for verses 19-21. Literal keeps "temple" for both words with the note.

decisions.choice: cattle
decisions.reason: "Oxen" now suggests animals that pull ploughs; these were cattle for sacrifice.

decisions.choice: for sacrifices
decisions.reason: Readable says why animals were sold in the temple (m2).

decisions.choice: a house of business
decisions.reason: Keeps the repeated word "house", which sets God's house against a trading house.

records.greek: ἐμνήσθησαν οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ ὅτι γεγραμμένον ἐστίν· Ὁ ζῆλος τοῦ οἴκου σου καταφάγεταί με.
records.gloss: Remembered the disciples of him that written it is, "The zeal of the house of you will eat up me."

L.17: His disciples remembered that it is written, "The zeal for Your house will eat Me up."

R.17: His disciples remembered that the Scripture says, "My strong love for Your house will consume Me."

decisions.choice: Psalm 69:10
decisions.reason: The words come from Psalm 69, the prayer of a righteous man who suffers for his loyalty to God. John quotes the same psalm at 15:25 and alludes to it at the cross (19:28-29).

decisions.choice: future: will consume me
decisions.reason: In Psalm 69:10 the verb is past. John's form is future, pointing ahead: Jesus's devotion to God's house will cost him his life.

decisions.choice: zeal: burning devotion to God's honor
decisions.reason: The word is used of passionate loyalty to God (compare Numbers 25:11, where Phinehas is zealous for God's honor), not of envy.

decisions.choice: they remembered it then, as they watched
alternatives: they remembered it only after the resurrection, like verse 22
decisions.reason: Verse 22 explicitly says "when he was raised"; this verse does not, so it most likely describes their thought at the time. Either is possible.

decisions.choice: eat me up (L); devour (B); consume (R)
decisions.reason: The verb is literally "eat up". Literal and Balanced keep the image of eating; Readable uses the plainest word for being used up.

decisions.choice: My strong love for
decisions.reason: "Zeal" is an uncommon word for young readers; Readable says what it means and makes "my" explicit, since the zeal is the speaker's.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθησαν οὖν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι καὶ εἶπαν αὐτῷ· Τί σημεῖον δεικνύεις ἡμῖν, ὅτι ταῦτα ποιεῖς;
records.gloss: Answered therefore the Jews and said to him, "What sign show you to us, that these things you do?"

L.18: So the Jews answered and said to Him, "What sign do You show us, since You do these things?"

R.18: Then the Jewish leaders in the temple asked Him, "What sign can You give us to show that You have the right to do this?"

decisions.choice: the Jews: the temple authorities in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: They demand to know by what right he acts in the temple, which is the authorities' question (compare 1:19, where priests and Levites are sent from Jerusalem, and Mark 11:27-28). It is not the Jewish people as a whole: Jesus, his disciples and the worshipers are Jews.

decisions.choice: responded to what he had done
decisions.reason: No one has asked anything; "answered" here means they reacted to his actions.

decisions.choice: a sign that would show his right to do these things
alternatives: what sign do you show, because you do these things?
decisions.reason: The clause gives the reason a sign is needed: since he acts with such authority, he must prove it. John's signs are given, not produced on demand (compare 6:30).

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς καὶ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον καὶ ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις ἐγερῶ αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Answered Jesus and said to them, "Destroy the temple this, and in three days I will raise it."

L.19: Jesus answered and said to them, "Tear down this temple, and in three days I will raise it up."

R.19: Jesus answered, "If you tear down this temple, I will raise it up again in three days."

decisions.choice: the sanctuary: the house of God itself
decisions.reason: Jesus uses the word for the sanctuary building where God's presence dwelt, not the word used in verses 14-15 for the whole temple area. Verse 21 uses the same word of his body.

decisions.choice: a command with the force of a condition: if you destroy it
decisions.reason: The command is a challenge, not a wish: if they destroy it, he will raise it. Either way the destroyers are the hearers. Mark 14:58 and 15:29 show that his words were later twisted against him.

decisions.choice: raise: used both of putting up a building and of raising the dead
decisions.reason: The verb has both senses, and verse 22 uses it of the resurrection. Every level keeps "raise" so the double meaning stays.

decisions.choice: Tear down
decisions.reason: The verb means to undo or pull down; for a building "tear down" is the natural word. It departs from the familiar "destroy", which also fits.

decisions.choice: If you tear down
decisions.reason: Readable states the condition the command implies (m2), so it does not sound like an invitation.

records.greek: εἶπαν οὖν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι· Τεσσεράκοντα καὶ ἓξ ἔτεσιν οἰκοδομήθη ὁ ναὸς οὗτος, καὶ σὺ ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις ἐγερεῖς αὐτόν;
records.gloss: Said therefore the Jews, "Forty and six years was built the temple this, and you in three days will raise it?"

L.20: So the Jews said, "[In] forty-six years this temple was built, and You will raise it up in three days?"

R.20: The Jewish leaders said, "People have been building this temple for forty-six years! Will You really raise it up in three days?"

decisions.choice: the Jews: the same temple authorities as in verse 18
decisions.reason: They continue the exchange that began in verse 18.

decisions.choice: the temple has been under construction for forty-six years
alternatives: the sanctuary was completed forty-six years ago
it took forty-six years to build
decisions.reason: Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple about 20/19 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 15.380), and work went on for decades after this, so forty-six years from the start puts this Passover around AD 27/28. Since the work was still going on, the sense is most likely "has been under construction". But the sanctuary building itself was finished early, and the verb can also mean "was built" some time ago. The evidence is balanced.

decisions.choice: and you: an emphatic, scornful "you"
decisions.reason: The pronoun is stressed: forty-six years of work, and this man claims to do it in three days.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: As in verse 18.

decisions.choice: Will you really
decisions.reason: Readable shows the scorn of the emphatic pronoun (m3).

records.greek: ἐκεῖνος δὲ ἔλεγεν περὶ τοῦ ναοῦ τοῦ σώματος αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: That one however was speaking about the temple of the body of him.

L.21: But that one was speaking about the temple of His body.

R.21: But when Jesus said "temple", He was talking about His own body.

decisions.choice: the temple that is his body
alternatives: a temple belonging to his body
decisions.reason: The second noun says what the temple is: his body is the sanctuary.

decisions.choice: Jesus's body is the place where God dwells among people
decisions.reason: John has already said that the Word "pitched his tent" among us (1:14), as God's glory dwelt in the tabernacle. Now the sanctuary Jesus speaks of is himself; its destruction and raising are his death and resurrection (verse 22).

decisions.choice: that one, emphatic: he, unlike his hearers, meant something else
decisions.reason: John often lets hearers misunderstand Jesus and then explains (3:4; 4:11; 11:11-13).

decisions.choice: when Jesus said "temple"
decisions.reason: Readable names the word being explained so young readers can follow the double meaning.

records.greek: ὅτε οὖν ἠγέρθη ἐκ νεκρῶν, ἐμνήσθησαν οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ ὅτι τοῦτο ἔλεγεν, καὶ ἐπίστευσαν τῇ γραφῇ καὶ τῷ λόγῳ ὃν εἶπεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς.
records.gloss: When therefore he was raised from dead [ones], remembered the disciples of him that this he was saying, and they believed the Scripture and the word which said the Jesus.

L.22: So when He was raised out of [the] dead, His disciples remembered that He was saying this, and they believed the Scripture and the word which Jesus spoke.

R.22: Later, after Jesus was raised from the dead, His disciples remembered that He had said this. Then they believed the Scripture and what Jesus had said.

decisions.choice: he was raised: God raised him
decisions.reason: The passive points to God as the one who raised him (compare Acts 2:24). In John, Jesus also says he will raise the temple himself (2:19; 10:17-18); the Gospel holds both together, so every level keeps the passive.

decisions.choice: the Scripture: a particular passage, most likely Psalm 69:10 quoted in verse 17
alternatives: a passage about rising, such as Psalm 16:10
decisions.reason: John uses the singular for a particular passage (as in 7:38; 19:24). The nearest one is the psalm in verse 17, but John may mean Scripture's witness to the resurrection in general (20:9). The evidence is balanced.

decisions.choice: the disciples understood only after the resurrection
decisions.reason: John says the same in 12:16, and Jesus promises that the Spirit will remind them of all he said (14:26).

decisions.choice: believed the Scripture and his word: trusted that they were true
alternatives: believed in them as in a person
decisions.reason: Here the verb takes a plain object, not "in": they now trusted what Scripture and Jesus had said.

decisions.choice: Later
decisions.reason: Makes clear that John looks ahead to after the resurrection.

records.greek: Ὡς δὲ ἦν ἐν τοῖς Ἱεροσολύμοις ἐν τῷ πάσχα ἐν τῇ ἑορτῇ, πολλοὶ ἐπίστευσαν εἰς τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ, θεωροῦντες αὐτοῦ τὰ σημεῖα ἃ ἐποίει·
records.gloss: When then he was in the Jerusalem at the Passover at the feast, many believed in the name of him, seeing of him the signs which he was doing.

L.23: Now while He was in Jerusalem at the Passover, at the feast, many believed in His name, seeing His signs which He was doing.

R.23: While Jesus was in Jerusalem for the Passover festival, many people saw the signs He was doing, and they believed in Him.

decisions.choice: believed in his name: believed in him
decisions.reason: A name stands for the person, as in 1:12.

decisions.choice: their belief rested on the signs they watched
alternatives: they believed and also happened to see signs
decisions.reason: The participle gives the setting and the ground of their belief. John treats belief that rests only on signs as real but not yet deep (4:48; 20:29), and the next sentence shows its limit.

decisions.choice: signs John does not describe
decisions.reason: John has told only one sign so far, at Cana. These are others done in Jerusalem, which he mentions without telling (compare 20:30).

decisions.choice: believed in him
decisions.reason: Readable gives the meaning of the idiom (m1).

records.greek: αὐτὸς δὲ Ἰησοῦς οὐκ ἐπίστευεν αὑτὸν αὐτοῖς διὰ τὸ αὐτὸν γινώσκειν πάντας καὶ ὅτι οὐ χρείαν εἶχεν ἵνα τις μαρτυρήσῃ περὶ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, αὐτὸς γὰρ ἐγίνωσκεν τί ἦν ἐν τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ.
records.gloss: He himself however Jesus was not believing himself to them, because of the him knowing all [people], \v 25 and because not need he had that anyone should testify about the human being; he himself for knew what was in the human being.

L.24: But Jesus Himself was not entrusting Himself to them, because He knew all people,
L.25: and because He had no need that anyone should testify about a human being, for He Himself knew what was in a human being.

R.24: But Jesus would not trust them, because He knew all people.
R.25: No one needed to tell Him what people are like. He already knew what was in their hearts.

decisions.choice: entrust himself: commit himself to them, rely on them
decisions.reason: This is the same verb as "believed" in verse 23. With an object and a person it means to entrust something to someone (Luke 16:11). John plays on the two senses: many believed in him, but he did not entrust himself to them. Since one word cannot carry both senses here, a footnote points out the wordplay.

decisions.choice: all people
decisions.reason: The masculine plural is general here, as verse 25 shows by speaking of people in general.

decisions.choice: a human being, people in general
decisions.reason: The word is used in the general sense, so the gender setting applies.

decisions.choice: he knew what was in people
decisions.reason: Knowing the heart belongs to God (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10). John has just shown it with Nathanael (1:47-48) and will show it again with the Samaritan woman (4:18, 29). The next chapter begins with "a man", using the same word, Nicodemus, as an example.

decisions.choice: entrust himself (L); trust himself to them (B); trust them (R)
decisions.reason: The verb cannot be "believe" here and still make sense. "Trust" keeps as much of the echo of verse 23 as possible; Readable says the plain meaning.

decisions.choice: {{gender:all people|all men}}; {{gender:a person|man}}
decisions.reason: Inclusive default; Traditional one tap away.

decisions.choice: what was in their hearts
decisions.reason: Readable names the inner life, which "what was in" a person means.
